label: What is AIRFLOW?
title: Design the
conditions for
better work.
cues: What helps people do meaningful work today and still have the capacity to improve it tomorrow?
AIRFLOW is a framework for designing the conditions in which people, collective intelligence, and organizations can flourish together.

label: Why it matters
title: Better tools.
Same bottleneck?
cues: Imagine a team that uses AI to draft reports faster.
If reviewers spend longer checking the claims, the queue may simply move.
AIRFLOW follows the whole job, including who does the work and what capacity it leaves for the future.

label: Where the language comes from
title: Four perspectives, one design question.
cues: Flow science asks what supports deep engagement.
Biomimicry asks how living systems sense, adapt, and renew.
Organizational development asks how roles and relationships shape what people can do.
Artificial intelligence asks where technology can support human judgement and coordination.

label: How a pattern is derived
title: From a recurring tension
to a move you can test.
cues: Start with a recurring situation. Identify what two legitimate needs are pulling against each other.
Use the four perspectives to ask what could change. For example, local sensing in nature prompts a question:
Could customer signals reach the team able to act? That is a design hypothesis to test in context.
The pattern records the context, the tension, a practical move, and the limits of its usefulness.

label: A pattern in practice
title: Protected Focus
cues: Say the work needs concentration, while colleagues still need an urgent response.
Agree a focus window, a named backup, and a clear exception for urgent requests.
Then check the quality of the work, how urgent requests were handled, and what the backup person had to absorb.

label: How to use the language
title: Start with one
real incident.
cues: Use the language to redesign a handover, clarify who can decide, or test how AI changes a workflow.
Choose one pattern that addresses the tension. Add another if you need to balance a trade-off.
Agree what to observe and when to review, revise, or stop. The patterns are working proposals.

label: Explore the language
title: Six families. Twenty-four patterns.
cues: The public guide organizes twenty-four patterns into six families.
Start with the problem you can describe. Each family gives you a different place to look.

label: AIRFLOW
title: What would make
better work possible?
cues: Pick a moment when meaningful work stalled. Ask what condition would make the next step easier.
Next in the series, we explore the six families and the icons that help you recognize them.
